claim: Next-generation and Sanger sequencing were combined to identify disease-causing USH2A mutations in an adult patient with autosomal recessive RP.
source: Next-generation and Sanger sequencing were combined to identify disease-causing USH2A mutations in an adult patient with autosomal recessive RP.
evidence: The abstract states this was done, and the Results section describes the sequencing experiments performed.

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) were generated from the patient's keratinocytes.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), generated from the patient's keratinocytes, were differentiated into multi-layer eyecup-like structures with features of human retinal precursor cells.
evidence: The abstract and Results section describe the generation of iPSCs from keratinocytes, with Figure 1 showing the process.

claim: iPSCs were differentiated into multi-layer eyecup-like structures with features of human retinal precursor cells.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), generated from the patient's keratinocytes, were differentiated into multi-layer eyecup-like structures with features of human retinal precursor cells.
evidence: Figure 2 shows the morphological development of eyecup-like structures with distinct layers.

claim: The inner layer of the eyecups contained photoreceptor precursor cells that expressed photoreceptor markers.
source: The inner layer of the eyecups contained photoreceptor precursor cells that expressed photoreceptor markers and exhibited axonemes and basal bodies characteristic of outer segments.
evidence: Figure 4 shows immunocytochemical analysis demonstrating expression of recoverin and rhodopsin in neural rosettes.

claim: Photoreceptor precursor cells exhibited axonemes and basal bodies characteristic of outer segments.
source: The inner layer of the eyecups contained photoreceptor precursor cells that expressed photoreceptor markers and exhibited axonemes and basal bodies characteristic of outer segments.
evidence: Figure 4B shows TEM analysis revealing cilia with clearly identifiable basal bodies.

claim: One of the patient's mutations causes exonification of intron 40, a translation frameshift and a premature stop codon.
source: Analysis of the USH2A transcripts of these cells revealed that one of the patient's mutations causes exonification of intron 40, a translation frameshift and a premature stop codon.
evidence: Figure 6A shows RT-PCR analysis demonstrating the introduction of a pseudoexon from intron 40.

claim: Western blotting revealed upregulation of GRP78 and GRP94, suggesting that the patient's other USH2A variant (Arg4192His) causes disease through protein misfolding and ER stress.
source: Western blotting revealed upregulation of GRP78 and GRP94, suggesting that the patient's other USH2A variant (Arg4192His) causes disease through protein misfolding and ER stress.
evidence: Figure 6C shows Western blot analysis demonstrating elevated expression of GRP78 and GRP94 in the proband compared to controls.

claim: Transplantation into 4-day-old immunodeficient Crb1−/− mice resulted in the formation of morphologically and immunohistochemically recognizable photoreceptor cells.
source: Transplantation into 4-day-old immunodeficient Crb1−/− mice resulted in the formation of morphologically and immunohistochemically recognizable photoreceptor cells, suggesting that the mutations in this patient act via post-developmental photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: Figure 7 shows immunocytochemical analysis of transplanted cells expressing human markers and photoreceptor markers in mouse retina.

claim: The mutations in this patient act via post-developmental photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Transplantation into 4-day-old immunodeficient Crb1−/− mice resulted in the formation of morphologically and immunohistochemically recognizable photoreceptor cells, suggesting that the mutations in this patient act via post-developmental photoreceptor degeneration.
evidence: The successful integration and differentiation of patient cells into photoreceptors suggests the mutations do not prevent photoreceptor development.

claim: Mutations in the USH2A gene are the most common cause of Usher syndrome type I.
source: Mutations in the USH2A gene are the most common cause of Usher syndrome type I (Aller et al., 2006; Baux et al., 2007; DePristo et al., 2011) and are also a common cause of non-syndromic RP (McGee et al., 2010; Vaché et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: USH2A mutations are a common cause of non-syndromic RP.
source: Mutations in the USH2A gene are the most common cause of Usher syndrome type I (Aller et al., 2006; Baux et al., 2007; DePristo et al., 2011) and are also a common cause of non-syndromic RP (McGee et al., 2010; Vaché et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The large size of the USH2A gene precludes the use of the types of viral vectors currently employed for retinal gene therapy.
source: The obstacles to such treatment include the large size of the USH2A gene, which precludes the use of the types of viral vectors currently employed for retinal gene therapy.
evidence: This is stated as a known obstacle based on the gene size and viral vector packaging limitations.

claim: The reprogramming of keratinocytes has been shown to be as much as 100-fold more efficient and at least twofold faster than the reprogramming of dermal fibroblasts.
source: Of the accessible cell types used for iPSC generation, the reprogramming of keratinocytes has been shown to be as much as 100-fold more efficient and at least twofold faster than the reprogramming of dermal fibroblasts (Aasen et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Aasen et al., 2008.

claim: Keratinocyte-derived iPSCs are more similar to embryonic stem cells than those generated from fibroblasts.
source: In addition, it has recently been shown that keratinocyte-derived iPSCs are more similar to embryonic stem cells than those generated from fibroblasts (Barrero et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Barrero et al., 2012.

claim: The post-mitotic photoreceptor precursor cell is the optimal cell type for efficient rod photoreceptor cell replacement.
source: Work from Ali et al. clearly demonstrates that the post-mitotic photoreceptor precursor cell is the optimal cell type for efficient rod photoreceptor cell replacement (Lakowski et al., 2011; Pearson et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to work from Ali et al.

claim: Exome sequencing of the patient yielded 71 million uniquely mapped paired-end sequences, each end 50 bp in length.
source: This experiment yielded 71 million uniquely mapped paired-end sequences, each end 50 bp in length.
evidence: This is a direct report of the sequencing data obtained.

claim: More than 20,000 sequence variations were detected in the patient's exome.
source: More than 20,000 sequence variations were detected (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a direct report of the number of variants detected.

claim: After applying filters to the exome data, more than 400 plausible disease-causing sequence variations, in more than 300 genes, remained for further consideration.
source: After applying these filters to the data, more than 400 plausible disease-causing sequence variations, in more than 300 genes, remained for further consideration.
evidence: This is a direct report of the filtering results.

claim: Two human retinal degeneration genes (ABCA4 and USH2A) each harbored a single plausible disease-causing variant.
source: There were no instances of two plausible disease-causing variants in a gene previously associated with RP, but two human retinal degeneration genes (ABCA4 and USH2A) each harbored a single plausible disease-causing variant (Thr1428Met ACG>ATG and Arg4192His CGC>CAC, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct report of the exome sequencing findings.

claim: Sanger sequencing of the entire coding sequence of ABCA4 and USH2A confirmed the presence of the heterozygous variants identified by exome sequencing but failed to detect a second disease-causing variation in either gene.
source: Sanger sequencing of the entire coding sequence of both of these genes confirmed the presence of the heterozygous variants identified by exome sequencing but failed to detect a second disease-causing variation in either gene.
evidence: This is a direct report of the Sanger sequencing validation results.

claim: A second RP patient with the Arg4192His variant in USH2A had a second well-established disease-causing mutation on the opposite USH2A allele.
source: First, we discovered a second RP patient with the Arg4192His variant in USH2A, and this individual had a second well-established disease-causing mutation on the opposite USH2A allele.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from screening additional RP patients.

claim: Vaché et al. (2012) published their discovery of a disease-causing variant in intron 40 of USH2A.
source: More importantly, Vaché et al. (2012) published their discovery of a disease-causing variant in intron 40 of USH2A.
evidence: This is a reference to a published finding by another group.

claim: Sanger sequencing of intron 40 in the patient revealed the intronic variant to be present in trans to his Arg4192His mutation.
source: Sanger sequencing of intron 40 in our patient revealed this intronic variant to be present in trans to his Arg4192His mutation.
evidence: This is a direct report of the Sanger sequencing results for intron 40.

claim: Passage-4 keratinocytes were plated at a density of 30,000 cells/cm2 and transduced with the transcription factors OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and C-MYC for iPSC generation.
source: For iPSC generation, passage-4 cells were plated at a density of 30,000 cells/cm2 and transduced with the transcription factors OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and C-MYC.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental protocol used.

claim: 2–3 weeks following the initial passage, small, morphologically distinct cell clusters were present.
source: 2–3 weeks following the initial passage, small, morphologically distinct cell clusters were present (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows early iPSC colonies at 2-3 weeks post-transduction.

claim: rt-PCR analysis confirmed expression of the pluripotency markers DNMT, LIN28, OCT4, KLF4, SOX2, Nanog, and C-MYC in iPSCs.
source: rt-PCR analysis confirmed expression of the pluripotency markers DNMT, LIN28, OCT4, KLF4, SOX2, Nanog, and C-MYC (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows RT-PCR bands for these pluripotency markers.

claim: Histologic analysis of teratomas revealed tissues specific to each of the three embryonic germ layers.
source: Histologic analysis of teratomas revealed tissues specific to each of the three embryonic germ layers (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Figure 1E and F show H&E staining of teratomas with tissues from all three germ layers.

claim: Immunohistochemical staining of teratomas revealed GFAP positive neural tissue and αSMA positive vascular structures.
source: Similarly, immunohistochemical staining revealed GFAP positive neural tissue (Figure 1G) and αSMA positive vascular structures (Figure 1H).
evidence: Figure 1G and H show immunostaining for GFAP and αSMA in teratomas.

claim: Retinal differentiation in mouse can be accomplished in 30 days.
source: Although retinal differentiation in mouse can be accomplished in 30 days (Tucker et al., 2011, 2013), retinal differentiation of human cells takes significantly longer.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Retinal differentiation of human cells takes significantly longer than mouse cells.
source: Although retinal differentiation in mouse can be accomplished in 30 days (Tucker et al., 2011, 2013), retinal differentiation of human cells takes significantly longer.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the current study.

claim: Keratinocyte-derived iPSCs formed eyecup-like structures with clearly defined layers of pigmented RPE and non-pigmented neural retina.
source: During differentiation, these keratinocyte-derived iPSCs formed eyecup-like structures with clearly defined layers of pigmented RPE and non-pigmented neural retina (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: Figure 2B-E shows the morphological development of eyecup structures with distinct layers.

claim: Fibroblast-derived iPSCs never develop eyecup-like structures under very similar culture conditions.
source: This was a clear departure from our previous experience with fibroblast-derived iPSCs, which never develop eyecup-like structures under very similar culture conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an observation comparing keratinocyte-derived and fibroblast-derived iPSCs.

claim: The eyecups began as small pigmented foci that could be detected as early as 45 days post-differentiation.
source: The eyecups began as small pigmented foci that could be detected as early as 45 days post-differentiation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows early pigmented structures at 45 days.

claim: Following passage and continued differentiation, pigmented clumps expanded and elongated over 150 days.
source: Following passage and continued differentiation, these pigmented clumps expanded and elongated over 150 days (Figure 2C) and were eventually joined by a clump of neural rosettes (Figure 2C, arrow) on one side of the pigmented structure.
evidence: Figure 2C shows the extended pigmented structures with neural rosettes.

claim: In some cases, RPE/neural units extended into C-shaped eyecup-like structures.
source: In some cases, these RPE/neural units extended into C-shaped eyecup-like structures (Figure 2D,E) while in others, the central cavity did not form and the structure consisted of a circular sheet of neural cells surrounded by a pigmented epithelium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2D and E show C-shaped eyecup structures.

claim: In many cases, multiple eyecups at different developmental stages were present within the same well of a differentiating six-well plate.
source: In many cases, multiple eyecups at different developmental stages were present within the same well of a differentiating six-well plate (Figure 2D, arrows).
evidence: Figure 2D shows multiple eyecups in a single well.

claim: 24 hr after plating RPE biopsies, pigment-containing cell clusters adhered to the culture surface and began to give rise to non-pigmented cells with a fibroblastic morphology.
source: 24 hr after plating, pigment-containing cell clusters adhered to the culture surface and began to give rise to non-pigmented cells with a fibroblastic morphology (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows RPE cells 24 hours after plating with fibroblastic morphology.

claim: By 72–96 hr post-plating, extensive cell spreading and a complete loss of pigmentation was noted in RPE cultures.
source: By 72–96 hr post-plating, extensive cell spreading and a complete loss of pigmentation was noted (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows RPE cells at 72 hours with loss of pigmentation.

claim: By 2 weeks post-plating, confluent cultures of densely pigmented hexagonal epithelial cells were present in RPE cultures.
source: By 2 weeks post-plating, confluent cultures of densely pigmented hexagonal epithelial cells were present (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D shows confluent RPE monolayer with typical cuboidal morphology and pigmentation.

claim: Immunocytochemical analysis revealed RPE cells expressing the tight junction marker ZO1.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of these cultures revealed cells expressing the tight junction marker ZO1 (Figure 3E), the transcription factor PAX6 (Figure 3F), the RPE-specific channel bestrophin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the RPE visual cycle protein RPE65 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 3E shows ZO1 immunostaining of RPE cells.

claim: Immunocytochemical analysis revealed RPE cells expressing the transcription factor PAX6.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of these cultures revealed cells expressing the tight junction marker ZO1 (Figure 3E), the transcription factor PAX6 (Figure 3F), the RPE-specific channel bestrophin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the RPE visual cycle protein RPE65 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 3F shows PAX6 immunostaining of RPE cells.

claim: Immunocytochemical analysis revealed RPE cells expressing the RPE-specific channel bestrophin.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of these cultures revealed cells expressing the tight junction marker ZO1 (Figure 3E), the transcription factor PAX6 (Figure 3F), the RPE-specific channel bestrophin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the RPE visual cycle protein RPE65 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows bestrophin immunostaining of RPE cells.

claim: Immunocytochemical analysis revealed RPE cells expressing the RPE visual cycle protein RPE65.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis of these cultures revealed cells expressing the tight junction marker ZO1 (Figure 3E), the transcription factor PAX6 (Figure 3F), the RPE-specific channel bestrophin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and the RPE visual cycle protein RPE65 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1B shows RPE65 immunostaining of RPE cells.

claim: TEM analysis showed that cells within the pigmented layer contained pigment granules, tight junctions with neighboring cells, and apical microvilli, all of which are characteristic of native RPE.
source: As shown in Figure 3, cells within the pigmented layer contained pigment granules (G, asterisks), tight junctions with neighboring cells (G and H, arrows), and apical microvilli (G and H, arrowheads), all of which are characteristic of native RPE.
evidence: Figure 3G and H show TEM images of RPE cells with these characteristic features.

claim: The pigmented layer of cells located at the perimeter of patient-specific eyecups is patient-specific RPE.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the pigmented layer of cells located at the perimeter of patient-specific eyecups is patient-specific RPE.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the morphological, immunocytochemical, and TEM analyses presented.

claim: Densely packed neural rosettes contained polarized recoverin positive cells.
source: Densely packed neural rosettes contained polarized recoverin positive cells (Figure 4C,E,F, and H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, green) with acetylated tubulin (Figure 4D,E, red) and rhodopsin (Figure 4G,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, red) positive structures concentrated at the luminal surface of the rosettes.
evidence: Figure 4 shows immunostaining for recoverin in neural rosettes.

claim: Neural rosettes had acetylated tubulin and rhodopsin positive structures concentrated at the luminal surface.
source: Densely packed neural rosettes contained polarized recoverin positive cells (Figure 4C,E,F, and H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, green) with acetylated tubulin (Figure 4D,E, red) and rhodopsin (Figure 4G,H, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, red) positive structures concentrated at the luminal surface of the rosettes.
evidence: Figure 4 shows immunostaining for acetylated tubulin and rhodopsin at the luminal surface of rosettes.

claim: TEM analysis confirmed the existence of cilia with clearly identifiable basal bodies in neural rosettes.
source: TEM analysis further confirmed the existence of cilia with clearly identifiable basal bodies (Figure 4B, arrowhead).
evidence: Figure 4B shows TEM image with basal bodies indicated.

claim: The retinal transcripts PAX6, OTX2, CRX, NRL, recoverin, and rhodopsin were detected in differentiating patient-specific iPSCs as early as 60 days post-differentiation.
source: The retinal transcripts PAX6, OTX2, CRX, NRL, recoverin, and rhodopsin were detected in differentiating patient-specific iPSCs as early as 60 days post-differentiation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows RT-PCR bands for these retinal transcripts at 60 days.

claim: The mature rod photoreceptor protein recoverin was not detected until 90 days post-differentiation.
source: However, the mature rod photoreceptor protein recoverin and the rod photopigment rhodopsin were not detected until 90 and 120 days post-differentiation, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows Western blot with recoverin first appearing at 90 days.

claim: The rod photopigment rhodopsin was not detected until 120 days post-differentiation.
source: However, the mature rod photoreceptor protein recoverin and the rod photopigment rhodopsin were not detected until 90 and 120 days post-differentiation, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows Western blot with rhodopsin first appearing at 120 days.

claim: The cone photopigments blue opsin and red/green opsin were first detected at 90 and 120 days post-differentiation, respectively.
source: Similarly, the cone photopigments blue opsin and red/green opsin were first detected at 90 and 120 days post-differentiation, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows Western blot with blue opsin at 90 days and red/green opsin at 120 days.

claim: RNA isolated from patient-specific iPSC-derived photoreceptor precursor cells revealed that the suspected splice site mutation identified in intron 40 caused exonification of the intron.
source: As shown in Figure 6, RNA isolated from patient-specific iPSC-derived photoreceptor precursor cells revealed that the suspected splice site mutation identified in intron 40 of the proband caused exonification of the intron (Figure 6A).
evidence: Figure 6A shows RT-PCR and sequencing demonstrating the introduction of intronic sequence.

claim: Introduction of intronic sequence between exons 40 and 41 results in a frame shift and introduction of a premature stop codon.
source: Introduction of intronic sequence between exons 40 and 41 results in a frame shift and introduction of a premature stop codon.
evidence: This is stated as the consequence of the exonification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Sanger sequencing of rt-PCR products confirmed the single point mutation identified within exon 63 of the patient's DNA.
source: Similarly, Sanger sequencing of rt-PCR products generated from the iPSC-derived photoreceptor precursor cells allowed us to confirm the single point mutation identified within exon 63 of the patients' DNA (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows sequencing traces confirming the Arg4192His mutation.

claim: The proband was found to have increased expression of the markers GRP78 and GRP94 indicative of protein misfolding and subsequent ER stress.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, when compared to normal human retina, iPSC-derived photoreceptor precursor cells from a normal control and a separate RP patient with known disease-causing mutations and pathophysiology (MAK associated RP caused by nonsense mediated decay of the transcript), the proband was found to have increased expression of the markers GRP78 and GRP94 indicative of protein misfolding and subsequent ER stress (Obeng et al., 2006; Lind et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 6C shows Western blot with elevated GRP78 and GRP94 in the proband, and citations support the interpretation of ER stress.

claim: The optimal cell type for retinal transplantation is the post-mitotic photoreceptor precursor cell.
source: It has been previously shown that the optimal cell type for retinal transplantation is the post-mitotic photoreceptor precursor cell (MacLaren et al., 2006; Pearson et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 2 weeks after plating, post-mitotic rhodopsin kinase positive photoreceptor precursor cells were abundant.
source: 2 weeks after plating, post-mitotic rhodopsin kinase positive photoreceptor precursor cells were abundant (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Figure 7A and B show rhodopsin kinase GFP expression in photoreceptor precursor cells.

claim: Clusters of rhodopsin kinase positive cells realigned in a polarized photoreceptor cell fashion and extended axon-like projections and outer-segment-like processes.
source: In many instances, clusters of the rhodopsin kinase positive cells realigned in a polarized photoreceptor cell fashion and extended axon-like projections (Figure 7B, arrowhead) and outer-segment-like processes (Figure 7B, arrow).
evidence: Figure 7B shows cells with axon-like and outer-segment-like projections indicated.

claim: Crb1−/− mice were chosen as recipient animals because they exhibit a relatively slow retinal degeneration and are more conducive to cellular integration with proper rod photoreceptor morphology following transplantation than other retinal degenerative strains.
source: Crb1−/− mice were chosen as recipient animals because they exhibit a relatively slow retinal degeneration and also because they are known to be more conducive to cellular integration with proper rod photoreceptor morphology following transplantation than other retinal degenerative strains (Barber et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Barber et al., 2013.

claim: 2 weeks after transplantation, extensive cellular integration was detected using the human Tra-1-85 blood antigen as a marker of human cells.
source: 2 weeks after transplantation, extensive cellular integration was detected using the human Tra-1-85 blood antigen as a marker of human cells (Figure 7C–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Sham injection control, red).
evidence: Figure 7C-F shows Tra-1-85 positive cells integrated in the mouse retina.

claim: The integrated cells expressed the mature photoreceptor marker recoverin.
source: The integrated cells expressed the mature photoreceptor marker recoverin, extended axonal projections toward the inner plexiform layer (Figure 7D–F arrowheads), and developed inner- and outer-segment-like projections that extended toward the underlying RPE layer (Figure 7D–F arrows).
evidence: Figure 7D-F shows recoverin expression in integrated cells.

claim: The integrated cells extended axonal projections toward the inner plexiform layer.
source: The integrated cells expressed the mature photoreceptor marker recoverin, extended axonal projections toward the inner plexiform layer (Figure 7D–F arrowheads), and developed inner- and outer-segment-like projections that extended toward the underlying RPE layer (Figure 7D–F arrows).
evidence: Figure 7D-F shows axonal projections indicated by arrowheads.

claim: The integrated cells developed inner- and outer-segment-like projections that extended toward the underlying RPE layer.
source: The integrated cells expressed the mature photoreceptor marker recoverin, extended axonal projections toward the inner plexiform layer (Figure 7D–F arrowheads), and developed inner- and outer-segment-like projections that extended toward the underlying RPE layer (Figure 7D–F arrows).
evidence: Figure 7D-F shows segment-like projections indicated by arrows.

claim: Patient-specific iPSC-derived retinal cells are a valuable new tool for investigators seeking to understand and treat degenerative retinal diseases.
source: Patient-specific iPSC-derived retinal cells are a valuable new tool for investigators seeking to understand and treat degenerative retinal diseases.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the work presented.

claim: iPSC-derived retinal cells will allow scientists to explore the pathophysiology of human diseases in ways that were previously possible only in animal models.
source: These cells will allow scientists to explore the pathophysiology of human diseases in ways that were previously possible only in animal models.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the technology.

claim: iPSC-derived retinal cells will be useful for evaluating potential therapies ranging from high-throughput screens of small molecule drugs to the comparison of gene replacement constructs.
source: They will also be useful for evaluating potential therapies ranging from high-throughput screens of small molecule drugs to the comparison of gene replacement constructs containing different promoters or packaged in different vectors.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the technology.

claim: For rare autosomal recessive disorders such as USH2A-associated RP, there is often little statistical evidence for the pathogenicity of one or both of a patient's putative disease-causing mutations.
source: For rare autosomal recessive disorders such as USH2A-associated RP, there is often little statistical evidence for the pathogenicity of one or both of a patient's putative disease-causing mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about rare recessive disorders.

claim: iPSC-derived retinal cells may be useful for confirming the pathogenicity of an unusual genotype before embarking upon an invasive therapy like subretinal administration of viral-mediated gene therapy.
source: In such cases, iPSC-derived retinal cells may be useful for confirming the pathogenicity of an unusual genotype before embarking upon an invasive therapy like subretinal administration of viral-mediated gene therapy.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the technology demonstrated in this study.

claim: Non-exomic mutations are not an uncommon cause of recessive diseases.
source: Non-exomic mutations are not an uncommon cause of recessive diseases. In some instances (e.g., CEP290-associated LCA) they account for the largest proportion of disease-causing alleles (Stone, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and general knowledge.

claim: In CEP290-associated LCA, non-exomic mutations account for the largest proportion of disease-causing alleles.
source: In some instances (e.g., CEP290-associated LCA) they account for the largest proportion of disease-causing alleles (Stone, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stone, 2007.

claim: As the iPSC technology becomes more routine, the evaluation of RNA from iPSC-derived retina may become a common step in the analysis of exome sequencing data when two clearly disease-causing alleles cannot be identified in known disease genes.
source: As the iPSC technology becomes more routine, the evaluation of RNA from iPSC-derived retina may become a common step in the analysis of exome sequencing data when two clearly disease-causing alleles cannot be identified in known disease genes.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future application based on the current work.

claim: The patient's USH2A mutations resulted in an upregulation of the markers GRP78 and GRP94 indicative of protein misfolding and subsequent ER stress.
source: In combination, these mutations resulted in an upregulation of the markers GRP78 and GRP94 indicative of protein misfolding and subsequent ER stress.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The patient's USH2A mutations do not appear to cause a gross developmental abnormality of photoreceptor cells.
source: This finding is compatible with our patient's history of normal vision until the third decade of life; that is, his USH2A mutations do not appear to cause a gross developmental abnormality of photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the successful transplantation and differentiation of patient cells, combined with the patient's clinical history.

claim: This is the first time that photoreceptor precursor cells have been derived from an adult human RP patient and successfully transplanted into mice.
source: The transplantation of photoreceptor precursor cells derived from early postnatal retina or embryonic stem cells has been accomplished before by other groups (MacLaren et al., 2006; La Torre et al., 2012; Pearson et al., 2012), but to our knowledge, this is the first time that photoreceptor precursor cells have been derived from an adult human RP patient and successfully transplanted into mice.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding, with citations to previous related work.

claim: Much work remains to be done before such transplants could be considered evidence for the feasibility of sight-restoring iPSC-derived treatments in humans.
source: However, much work remains to be done before such transplants could be considered evidence for the feasibility of sight-restoring iPSC-derived treatments in humans.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat to the findings.

claim: Synaptic connectivity will need to be demonstrated ultrastructurally and electrophysiologically for clinical feasibility.
source: For example, synaptic connectivity will need to be demonstrated ultrastructurally and electrophysiologically, and useful vision in treated animals will need to be demonstrated with an array of psychophysical approaches.
evidence: This is stated as a future requirement for clinical translation.

claim: Useful vision in treated animals will need to be demonstrated with an array of psychophysical approaches.
source: For example, synaptic connectivity will need to be demonstrated ultrastructurally and electrophysiologically, and useful vision in treated animals will need to be demonstrated with an array of psychophysical approaches.
evidence: This is stated as a future requirement for clinical translation.

claim: Longevity of the transplanted cells will be important to demonstrate for clinical feasibility.
source: Longevity of the transplanted cells will be important to demonstrate as will the cells' lack of tumorigenicity.
evidence: This is stated as a future requirement for clinical translation.

claim: The cells' lack of tumorigenicity will be important to demonstrate for clinical feasibility.
source: Longevity of the transplanted cells will be important to demonstrate as will the cells' lack of tumorigenicity.
evidence: This is stated as a future requirement for clinical translation.

claim: For transplants to have practical clinical utility, it will be important to show that the transplanted cells can integrate and function in the retinas of animals with advanced stages of many different molecular types of retinal degeneration.
source: For such transplants to have practical clinical utility it will also be important to show that the transplanted cells can integrate and function in the retinas of animals with advanced stages of many different molecular types of retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a future requirement for clinical translation.

claim: The coding sequence of USH2A is >18 kb.
source: The coding sequence of USH2A is >18 kb, and the packaging limits of AAV and EIAV vectors are about 3 kb and 10 kb, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the gene size.

claim: The packaging limits of AAV and EIAV vectors are about 3 kb and 10 kb, respectively.
source: The coding sequence of USH2A is >18 kb, and the packaging limits of AAV and EIAV vectors are about 3 kb and 10 kb, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as known information about viral vector capacities.

claim: HSV1 vectors can accommodate inserts of up to 40 kb in size.
source: For genes such as USH2A, vectors with large carrying capacities such as HSV1, which can accommodate inserts of up to 40 kb in size (Thomas et al., 2003), may be useful.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2003.

claim: The proper stoichiometry of the delivered message will be critical for some genes.
source: In addition to the vector limitations, the proper stoichiometry of the delivered message will also be critical for some genes.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration for gene therapy.

claim: Patients with a truncated protein encoded by one allele and a misfolded protein encoded by the other may require a different promoter and multiplicity of infection than a patient who harbors two stop mutations in USH2A.
source: It is possible that patients like the one reported here, with a truncated protein encoded by one allele and a misfolded protein encoded by the other, may require a different promoter and multiplicity of infection than a different patient who harbors two stop mutations in USH2A.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about personalized gene therapy approaches.

claim: Patient-specific iPSC-derived retinal cells may be useful in choosing the optimal gene therapy strategy for each individual.
source: Patient-specific iPSC-derived retinal cells may be useful in choosing the optimal gene therapy strategy for each individual.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the technology.

claim: For late-stage USH2A-associated RP where significant photoreceptor cell loss has occurred, cell replacement strategies will be required to restore vision.
source: For late-stage USH2A-associated RP where significant photoreceptor cell loss has occurred, cell replacement strategies will be required to restore vision.
evidence: This is stated as a logical conclusion based on the extent of cell loss.

claim: In some cases, correcting the genetic defect responsible for the photoreceptor degeneration will be necessary before transplanting photoreceptor cells into the patient.
source: In some cases, correcting the genetic defect responsible for the photoreceptor degeneration will be necessary before transplanting photoreceptor cells into the patient.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration for cell replacement therapy.

claim: TALEN- or CRISPR-based genome editing approaches allow for the targeted correction of patient-specific cells in vitro.
source: The development of site specific TALEN- or CRISPR-based genome editing approaches, which allow for the targeted correction of patient-specific cells in vitro, is proving to have great utility for endogenous gene correction (Hockemeyer et al., 2011; Ding et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent publications.

claim: Hockemeyer et al. demonstrated that for five genomic sites targeted, pluripotent iPSC clones carrying transgenes solely at TALEN-specified loci could be obtained.
source: For instance, Hockemeyer et al. recently demonstrated that for the five genomic sites targeted, pluripotent iPSC clones carrying transgenes solely at TALEN-specified loci could be obtained (Hockemeyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hockemeyer et al., 2011.

claim: Using the CRISPR/CAS-9 system, Wang et al. demonstrated the ability to simultaneously manipulate five separate genetic loci in mouse ES cells.
source: Similarly using the CRISPR/CAS-9 system, Wang et al. recently demonstrated the ability to simultaneously manipulate five separate genetic loci in mouse ES cells (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2013.

claim: TALEN- and CRISPR-mediated correction have the advantage that the gene remains under the control of the endogenous promoter.
source: A major advantage of these approaches is that unlike exogenous gene addition in which promoter strength and multiplicity of infection may require patient-specific adjustment, TALEN- and CRISPR-mediated correction have the advantage that the gene remains under the control of the endogenous promoter.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of genome editing approaches.

claim: For recessive diseases such as USH2A-associated RP, correction of a single disease-causing allele should be sufficient for a therapeutic effect.
source: For recessive diseases such as USH2A-associated RP, correction of a single disease-causing allele should be sufficient for a therapeutic effect.
evidence: This is stated based on the recessive nature of the disease.

claim: For some individuals with late-onset disease, genetic correction prior to transplantation may not be required.
source: It is possible that for some individuals with late-onset disease, such as the patient described in this report, genetic correction prior to transplantation may not be required.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the patient's clinical history.

claim: If the patient's native photoreceptor cells develop and function normally until the third decade of life, replacement of lost photoreceptors with iPSCs that have not been genetically modified could be a reasonably durable treatment.
source: That is, if the patient's native photoreceptor cells develop and function normally until the third decade of life, as suggested by our current data and the patient's clinical history, it is possible that replacement of lost photoreceptors with iPSCs that have not been genetically modified could be a reasonably durable treatment.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings and patient history.

claim: ES cell-derived retinal-pigmented epithelial cells are currently in clinical trial for the treatment of Stargardt macular dystrophy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
source: This approach is currently in clinical trial for the treatment of Stargardt macular dystrophy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2012.

claim: In ES cell-derived RPE clinical trials, cells are delivered to immune suppressed patients as subretinal bolus cell injections.
source: In these studies, ES cell-derived retinal-pigmented epithelial cells are delivered to immune suppressed patients as subretinal bolus cell injections (Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2012.

claim: Retinas injured by inherited disease often have a loss of integrity of the blood retinal barrier, which would allow the patient's peripheral immune system access to the transplanted cells.
source: Retinas injured by inherited disease often have a loss of integrity of the blood retinal barrier, which would allow the patient's peripheral immune system access to the transplanted cells.
evidence: This is stated as a known complication of retinal disease.

claim: Allogeneic cell transplant approaches would likely require life-long immunomodulation.
source: This type of transplant approach would likely require life-long immunomodulation, (Hambright et al., 2012) putting patients at further risk.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hambright et al., 2012.

claim: Keratinocytes cultured from a patient in the seventh decade of life can be reprogrammed into iPSCs.
source: We also demonstrated that keratinocytes cultured from a patient in the seventh decade of life can be reprogrammed into iPSCs and differentiated into a multi-layered eyecup-like structure with immunohistochemical and ultrastructural features of human retinal precursor cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful generation of iPSCs from the 62-year-old patient.

claim: Keratinocytes from a patient in the seventh decade of life can be differentiated into a multi-layered eyecup-like structure with immunohistochemical and ultrastructural features of human retinal precursor cells.
source: We also demonstrated that keratinocytes cultured from a patient in the seventh decade of life can be reprogrammed into iPSCs and differentiated into a multi-layered eyecup-like structure with immunohistochemical and ultrastructural features of human retinal precursor cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the differentiation experiments shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Patient-derived retinal precursor cells have the ability to integrate into the developing mouse retina and to form morphologically and immunohistochemically recognizable photoreceptor cells.
source: Finally, we showed that these patient-derived retinal precursor cells have the ability to integrate into the developing mouse retina and to form morphologically and immunohistochemically recognizable photoreceptor cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transplantation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: These findings will enable patient-specific studies of disease mechanism, gene correction, and photoreceptor cell transplantation for many different types of human retinal degeneration.
source: These findings will enable patient-specific studies of disease mechanism, gene correction, and photoreceptor cell transplantation for many different types of human retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the broader implications of the work.

claim: All experiments were conducted with the approval of the University of Iowa Animal Care and Use Committee and the University of Iowa Internal Review Board.
source: All experiments were conducted with the approval of the University of Iowa Animal Care and Use Committee (Animal welfare assurance #1009184) and the University of Iowa Internal Review Board (IRB # 200202022).
evidence: This is stated in the ethics statement.

claim: All experiments were consistent with the ARVO Statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research and the Treaty of Helsinki.
source: All experiments were consistent with the ARVO Statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research and the Treaty of Helsinki.
evidence: This is stated in the ethics statement.

claim: Skin biopsies were collected from a 62-year-old patient with an unknown cause of RP.
source: After informed consent, skin biopsies were collected from a 62-year-old patient with an unknown cause of RP, three patients with known causes of retinal disease and three individuals without eye disease, and these were used for fibroblast and keratinocyte isolation (as described previously [Bickenbach, 2005; Tucker et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: iPSCs were generated from human patient-specific keratinocytes via infection with four separate non-integrating Sendai viruses.
source: iPSCs were generated from human patient-specific keratinocytes via infection with four separate non-integrating Sendai viruses, each of which were designed to drive expression of one of four transcription factors: OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC (A1378001, Invitrogen, Grand Island, NY).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Keratinocytes were infected at an MOI of 5 for iPSC generation.
source: Keratinocytes plated on six-well tissue culture plates were infected at an MOI of 5.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: During reprogramming and maintenance of pluripotency, cells were cultured at 5% CO2, 5% O2, and 37°C.
source: During reprogramming and maintenance of pluripotency, cells were cultured at 5% CO2, 5% O2, and 37°C.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: To validate that generated iPSCs were pluripotent, teratomas were generated by IM injection of 2.5 × 106 undifferentiated iPSCs into immunodeficient (SCID) mice.
source: To validate that generated iPSCs were pluripotent, teratomas were generated by IM injection of 2.5 × 106 undifferentiated iPSCs into immunodeficient (SCID) mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: After 90 days, teratomas were excised, fixed, paraffin embedded, and sectioned.
source: After 90 days, tumors were excised, fixed, paraffin embedded, and sectioned.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Newly generated 150-day photoreceptor precursor cells were transplanted into the subretinal space of P4 immune compromised Rag1−/− x Crb1−/− mice.
source: Newly generated 150-day photoreceptor precursor cells were transplanted into the subretinal space of P4 immune compromised Rag1−/− x Crb1−/− mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 2 weeks after transplantation, mice were sacrificed and eyes were removed for histological analysis.
source: 2 weeks after transplantation, mice were sacrificed and eyes were removed for histological analysis, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 12 hr, embedded and sectioned on a cryostat.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
